lesson.title: Follow a relationship between tables

lead.text: Orders store a customer_id, and customers store the name. JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id pairs each order with the customer whose id matches.
An INNER JOIN keeps only the pairs that match.

steps.headline: A join pairs rows whose key values match.

lead.text: Orders refer to customers by number. Join the two tables on that number, and count the pairs that match.

reveal.text: You counted matching pairs, not names. Each order matched the one customer it refers to, so the rows still stand for orders.

queries.label: Order references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names attached
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

steps.headline: Which customers have placed an order?

queries.label: One row per match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Customers who ordered
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name;

workedSteps.text: Join customers to orders on c.id = o.customer_id.
workedSteps.math: one row for each matching pair

workedSteps.text: Look for customers with no pair.
SELECT DISTINCT c.name keeps each matched name once.

lead.text: CROSS JOIN has no condition. It pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.

reveal.text: You paired each customer with each order. That is not the same as the orders each customer placed.

queries.label: Match the reference
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every possible pair
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c CROSS JOIN orders AS o ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A join condition should follow the relationship the tables store. A condition that is not that relationship can match nothing, or the wrong rows.

queries.label: Paid matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Wrong columns
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.id ORDER BY o.id;

lesson.orientation: Join keys deliberately and account for every matching pair.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Each pupil has a club number: Ann 1, Bo 2, Cy 1 and Di 3. Club 1 is Chess.

intro.promise: By the end you'll join two tables on their key and say how many rows to expect.

recap.keyIdea: An INNER JOIN pairs rows whose keys match, so a row with no match disappears and a row with several matches repeats.

blocks.text: You matched 2 pupils to Chess, then counted 6 matching pairs between customers and orders. A cross join of the same tables gives 24.

recap.nextHook: Next, keep the customers who have no matching order.

questions.prompt: How many rows does the INNER JOIN of customers and orders on customer_id return?
hints: Count matches, not different names.
Ada, Ben and Cy each contribute two order matches.
Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matches; Dee contributes none to an inner join.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the six orders references one existing customer, so there are six matching pairs.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matching orders. Dee has none, so no pair holds her.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the different names. Count matching pairs instead.
That pairs every customer with every order. A join on the key pairs only matches.

questions.prompt: Why is Dee absent from the INNER JOIN result?
hints: An inner join requires a match.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An INNER JOIN retains only matching pairs. Dee has no matching order in this dataset, so her customer row contributes no result row.

choices.label: INNER JOIN keeps only the first customer

questions.onCorrect: She has no matching order. An inner join keeps only pairs that match.

misconceptions.feedback: Names do not affect matching. The key values do.
INNER JOIN keeps every pair that matches, not just one customer.

questions.prompt: How many pairs does CROSS JOIN produce for four customers and six orders?
hints: For each customer, include every order.
Multiply the table sizes.
Evaluate 4 × 6 for every possible customer-order pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every customer pairs with every order: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. A cross join pairs every customer with every order: 4 × 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two table sizes. A cross join pairs each row with every row of the other table.
That is the number of matching pairs. A cross join pairs every customer with every order.

questions.prompt: Which predicate follows the stored relationship?
hints: The order's customer_id refers to the customer's id.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: c.id = o.customer_id follows the customer reference stored on each order. Matching the two tables' unrelated id columns would connect the wrong records.

questions.onCorrect: c.id = o.customer_id. The order's customer_id holds the customer's key.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares a customer key with an order key. They are different things.
A name is not a stored reference to an item.

questions.prompt: Customers A, B and C have two, zero and one orders respectively. How many rows does their INNER JOIN return?
hints: An unmatched customer contributes no inner-join row.
Add the order matches.
Evaluate 2 + 0 + 1; each matching order contributes a row.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Each matching order is one row, and the customer with none adds nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts customers with orders. Each matching order is a row.

questions.prompt: Why can a customer's name repeat in a correctly joined result?
hints: A one-to-many relationship creates one row for each match.

acceptedIdeas: A person can match several orders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each matching customer-and-order pair produces a result row. A customer with several orders appears several times without the join being wrong.

choices.label: A person can match several orders
JOIN always duplicates every row twice
Names cannot be selected in SQL

questions.onCorrect: A person can match several orders. Each match gives its own row, so the name repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: Rows repeat once per match, and that number depends on the data.
Names are columns like any other and can be selected.

questions.prompt: How many pupils would a Chess list show?
hints: Which column connects a pupil to a club?
Find the pupils whose club number is the Chess number.
Count those pupils, not the clubs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Club 1 is Chess. Ann and Cy both have club number 1, so the list shows two pupils.

questions.onCorrect: 2. You followed a number from one list to the other. A join pairs rows by following keys like that.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the club. The list is of pupils.
That counts every pupil. Only those with the Chess number belong.

questions.prompt: A pupil row holds club = 2. The club ids are 1, 2 and 3. How many club rows does that pupil match in a join on the club number?
hints: Which club id equals the pupil's club number?
Compare the number with each club id in turn.
How many of the club ids are the same number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the club row whose id is 2 matches, so the pupil pairs with one club row.

questions.onCorrect: 1. A join pairs a row only with rows whose key value is equal to its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every club. The pupil matches only the club with its own number.

questions.prompt: Customers P, Q and R have 3, 1 and 0 orders. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT name over their INNER JOIN return?
hints: Which customers appear in the joined result at all?
A customer with no orders has no pair.
DISTINCT keeps each name once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: P and Q each have orders, so each appears. R has no pair. DISTINCT leaves two names.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Only customers with a match appear, and DISTINCT keeps each name once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the matching pairs. DISTINCT keeps each name once.
A customer with no orders has no pair, so no name appears for them.
